title: Jog out, run, then walk in
allegory: A learning-rate schedule is a runner's pacing plan for stopping exactly on a flag in the fog: jog out while you get your bearings, run hard across open ground, then slow to a walk as you close in, because at one fixed sprint you keep overshooting the flag.
map: jogging out while you get your bearings
warmup: small steps while early training is least stable
the peak rate, far from any minimum
slowing to a walk near the flag
annealing, so gradient noise stops knocking the weights around the minimum
a fixed sprint that keeps overshooting
a constant rate: the loss hovers in a noisy band and never settles

cap.1: Run at one fixed pace towards a flag in the fog and you keep overshooting it, back and forth. Training at one fixed learning rate does the same.
cap.2: With a constant learning rate, noisy minibatch gradients keep kicking the weights around the minimum. The loss drops, then hovers in a jittery band instead of settling.
cap.3: Under SGD noise, a constant step size leaves the parameters wandering in a region around the minimum whose size grows with the step size. Decaying the rate shrinks that region.

cap.1: Better plan: jog out while you get your bearings, run hard across open ground, then slow to a walk as the flag gets close. You stop right on it.
cap.2: A schedule changes the learning rate as training goes: small at first (warmup), large in the middle, shrinking at the end (annealing). Same optimizer, different step sizes over time.
cap.3: The schedule multiplies a base rate by a function of the step count, for example linear warmup then linear or cosine decay. The optimizer's update rule itself is unchanged.

cap.1: Across training the stride starts tiny, climbs to its peak, then shrinks back to nothing. The flat line is the one-pace runner.
cap.2: Linear warmup over the first slice of training, then linear decay to zero. In code the scheduler just sets a new lr each step; the optimizer never knows.
cap.3: lr(t) = peak·min(t/t_w, (T − t)/(T − t_w)): linear warmup until t_w, then linear anneal to 0 at step T. Cosine decay is a common smoother alternative.

chapters.name: Why warm up?

right.title: What research found
lines: for LayerNorm after the residual add

chapters.verdict: Keep a short warmup and anneal to zero; the why is still being argued.

cap.1: Nobody fully agrees why the slow start helps. What you need: a short warmup, then slow down to the end. Keep it; it is cheap.
cap.2: Warmup was standard transformer practice long before anyone had a mechanism for it. One answer: it guards against large early gradients when LayerNorm sits after the residual add. Keep a short one anyway.
cap.3: Xiong et al. (ICML 2020) traced the need for warmup to Post-LN placement: large gradients near the output at init. Pre-LN, as in GPT-2, makes it optional. Practical call: a short warmup costs little.

cap.1: In code the pacing plan is tiny: each step, write a new stride length into the optimizer. Different groups of weights can even run at different paces.
cap.2: A scheduler is a library call (e.g. torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR) that rewrites param_group['lr'] every step. This week's exercise builds the param groups it writes into.
cap.3: param_groups let one optimizer hold per-group hyperparameters (lr, momentum, weight decay). Most schedulers scale every group's base lr by the same factor, so the ratios between groups hold.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: PPO in [2.3]: anneal linearly to zero
Warm up, then anneal: the default shape

cap.1: In PPO, letting the rate fall to zero is one of a handful of details that decide whether CartPole gets solved. A small plan with a big effect.
cap.2: [2.3] anneals PPO's learning rate linearly to zero, one of the handful of details separating a run that solves CartPole from one that doesn't. Next week's sweeps then tune the peak rate.
cap.3: When you fine-tune or RL-train a model to steer its behaviour, the schedule decides whether updates settle or keep jittering. Treat the shape as a library default and tune the peak.

coda.title: Pace a toy training run and read the final loss

caption.1: Slide anneal to 0 and the loss ends in a jittery band; slide it to 1 and it settles lower. Then try a tiny peak: now slowing down only makes you late.
caption.2: Toy model: progress grows with the total distance stepped, jitter grows with the current step. Annealing trades a little progress for a quiet finish, which pays once the peak is big enough.
caption.3: A toy of SGD's two terms: optimisation error decays with Σ lr, noise scales with the current lr. Real curves differ, but this trade-off is why schedules end low. Warmup's stability benefit is not modelled.

where_else: PPO in [2.3]: the learning rate anneals linearly to zero
KL warm-up in VAEs: ramp the KL weight up from zero so the latent gets used first
L1 warmup when training sparse autoencoders, so latents are not killed early
Large-batch training, which pairs a scaled-up rate with a gradual warmup

hamming.what: A plan for changing the step size during training: small at first, largest early on, shrinking towards zero at the end.
hamming.when: Any training run long enough to settle, and especially transformers and PPO, whose standard recipes include one.
hamming.why: A fixed step either crawls or jitters around the minimum; a schedule buys speed early and a quiet, settled finish.

object.title: The pacing staircase
object.subtitle: Three pacing plans side by side, left to right through training: bar height is the stride.

cap.1: Three pacing plans laid side by side, left to right through training. Bar height is the stride length at that moment.
cap.2: Rows are schedules, columns are slices of training, height is the learning rate in that slice.
cap.3: Each row is lr(t) sampled at 12 points: constant, linear decay, and linear warmup plus linear decay.

cap.1: Turn annealing off and every plan keeps its stride to the very end: the runner who overshoots forever.
cap.2: With anneal at 0 the rate never falls, so late-training noise stays as large as mid-training noise.
cap.3: No decay means the stationary jitter around the minimum stays at its peak-rate size through the final step.

cap.1: The middle row starts at full stride and glides to zero. That is what [2.3] does to PPO's learning rate.
cap.2: Linear decay to zero with no warmup: PPO's schedule in [2.3], one of its standard implementation details.
cap.3: lr(t) = lr₀(1 − t/T). In [2.3] this separates PPO runs that solve CartPole from ones that do not.

cap.1: Stretch the warmup and the back row climbs a long gentle ramp before its peak. Safer early on, a bit slower overall.
cap.2: A longer warmup trades early progress for stability while the network is changing fastest.
cap.3: Warmup length is a stability-versus-speed trade-off; in Pre-LN transformers it can often be short.

cap.1: The usual recipe: a short climb, then a long glide down to zero. Pick it from a library and tune only the peak.
cap.2: Warmup then anneal is the default shape. Schedulers are library calls; sweeps tune the peak rate.
cap.3: In practice the schedule's shape is a default and the peak lr is the swept hyperparameter.

predict.q: The loss drops, then hovers in a jittery band that never settles. What is most likely to help?

options.t: Anneal the learning rate towards zero

predict.why: The jitter is noisy gradients times the step size. Shrinking the step at the end lets the weights settle.

predict.q: A scheduler changes the learning rate. What does it actually touch?

options.t: Each param group's lr, every step

predict.why: The optimizer's rule is unchanged. The scheduler rewrites param_group['lr'] as training goes.

predict.q: In [2.3], what does PPO's learning rate do over training?
predict.why: Linear annealing to zero is one of the standard PPO details that decides whether CartPole gets solved.

object.where: Any coefficient ramped over training: KL warm-up in VAEs, L1 warmup in sparse autoencoders, the learning rate in PPO.
